content.title: Dancing With Systems
content.excerpt: Remember that the goal is not to control the system, but to participate in its dance.
content.author: Donella Meadows
content.body:
Systems can’t be controlled, but they can be designed and redesigned. We can’t surge forward with certainty into a world of no surprises, but we can expect surprises and learn from them and even profit from them.

We can’t impose our will on a system. We can listen to what the system tells us, and discover how its properties and our values can work together to bring forth something much better than could ever be produced by our will alone.

Core Heuristics:

  • Get the beat of the system before you try to change it.
  • Expose your mental models to the light of day.
  • Honor and respect information above all else.
  • Locate responsibility in the system.
  • Stay humble — stay a learner.

content.title: Mountains and Waters
content.excerpt: Before one studies Zen, mountains are mountains and waters are waters; after a glimpse, mountains are no longer mountains; upon realization, mountains are once again mountains.
content.author: Dōgen Zenji
content.body:
In systems inquiry, the novice sees isolated components (reductionism). In intermediate inquiry, all boundaries dissolve into an undifferentiated sea of interconnectedness (holism).

In true systems consciousness—the third stage of Zen realization—boundaries and organs reappear. Not as isolated absolutes, but as relational membranes in dynamic equilibrium.

Form is emptiness; emptiness is form. The mountain stands solid precisely because it is fluidly continuous with the rain, the mantle, and the sky.

content.title: The Pattern Which Connects
content.excerpt: What pattern connects the crab to the lobster and the orchid to the primrose and all the four of them to me? And me to you?
content.author: Gregory Bateson
content.body:
Gregory Bateson in Mind and Nature argued that the foundational pathology of human thought is dividing the creature from its environment.

Mind is not located inside the cranium. Mind is the total recursive feedback circuit that flows through the creature, its physical environment, its motor actions, and its sensory reflections.

When you sever an ecological relationship, you do not damage an external object—you sever part of the neural circuitry of your own systemic anatomy.

galls-law-and-tao.title: Gall's Law & The Tao of Complexity

content.title: Gall's Law & The Tao of Complexity
content.excerpt: A complex system that works is invariably found to have evolved from a simple system that worked.
content.author: John Gall
content.body:
John Gall formulated the law of evolutionary simplicity:

A complex system designed from scratch never works and cannot be patched up to make it work. You have to start over with a working simple system.

This mirrors Chapter 64 of the Tao Te Ching:

A tree that can fill the span of a man's arms grows from a tiny sprout. A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step. Tackle the difficult while it is still easy; achieve great things through the smallest actions.

Bottom-up growth under continuous feedback produces enduring harmony; top-down unconstrained engineering produces collapse.

content.title: Equilibrium, Feedback, and Mind
content.excerpt: We are not the stuff that abides, but patterns that perpetuate themselves. A pattern is a message.
content.author: Norbert Wiener
content.body:
Norbert Wiener, the father of Cybernetics, recognized that all purposeful organisms, sculptures, and societies sustain their boundaries through balancing negative feedback loops.

Zen meditation is physical homeostatic regulation in its purest form: noticing divergence, relaxing tension, returning to the breath. When the feedback loop is frictionless, the system enters the state of pure living form.

content.title: Interbeing and Systems Wholeness
content.excerpt: If you are a poet, you will see clearly that there is a cloud floating in this sheet of paper.
content.author: Thich Nhat Hanh
content.body:
Thich Nhat Hanh formulated Interbeing to express Pratītyasamutpāda (dependent co-arising):

Without a cloud, there will be no rain; without rain, the trees cannot grow; and without trees, we cannot make paper. The cloud is essential for the paper to exist. If the cloud is not here, the sheet of paper cannot be here either. So we can say that the cloud and the paper inter-are.

In modern systems dynamics, this is the reality of stock-and-flow networks: every stock is an accumulation of flowing relationships with the whole biosphere.
